questions.q: The true class is Dog and the model gives it probability $0.5$. Using $\text{Loss} = -\ln(p_{\text{true}})$, what is the loss?
questions.explain: $-\ln 0.5 = \ln 2 \approx 0.693$ (nats). $1$ would be the value in bits ($-\log_2 0.5$); $0.301$ uses $\log_{10}$.

questions.q: In the Dog/Cat/Bird game the logits are $z = [2,\ 1,\ 0]$ and the actual image is a Dog. After softmax, what is the cross-entropy loss?
questions.explain: $p_{\text{Dog}} = e^2/(e^2 + e^1 + e^0) \approx 0.665$, so the loss is $-\ln 0.665 \approx 0.41$. $0.67$ is the probability itself, not the loss; the loss is never negative.

questions.q: With $p = \sigma(z)$ and true label $y = 1$, the model is confidently wrong at $p = 0.01$. How do the gradients w.r.t. $z$ compare?
options: Both are about the same size
Both are exactly $0$ because the model is saturated
questions.explain: The sigmoid's flattening multiplies MSE's gradient by $p(1-p)$, which is tiny here. Cross-entropy cancels that factor, so the learning signal stays strong exactly when the model is most wrong.

questions.q: With a one-hot target, which probabilities does cross-entropy **directly** penalize?
options: Only the probability of the true class; other classes matter only because they steal probability from it
questions.explain: $-\sum_k y_k \ln p_k$ keeps only the true-class term $-\ln p_{\text{true}}$. Because softmax probabilities sum to 1, raising a wrong class lowers $p_{\text{true}}$ and thereby raises the loss.
